title: Does Head Start Improve Children's Life Chances? Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design
research_question: Does participation in Head Start produce lasting improvements in children's life outcomes, specifically their health (as measured by child mortality from causes addressable by the program's health services) and their long-term educational attainment? To what extent do any benefits extend to both black and white children in very poor areas?
data_description: The study combines several county-level and individual-level datasets. County-level sources include a 1964 Census Bureau re-tabulation of 1960 county poverty rates (obtained from the National Archives), OEO records of federal program expenditures by county for 1968 and 1972, the Vital Statistics Compressed Mortality Files for 1973–1983 (with cause-of-death and age detail used to construct mortality rates for children ages 5–9 from causes plausibly affected by Head Start health services), a special tabulation of the 1990 Census providing educational attainment by county, age group, gender, and race, and biannual county voter registration data from 1968–1980. Individual-level data come from a restricted, geo-coded version of the National Education Longitudinal Study of 1988 (NELS), tracking 8th graders through 2000 (around age 25), with parent-reported Head Start participation and county of residence at age 13. The ECLS-K and PSID are used in supporting analyses. The unit of observation is primarily the U.S. county.
institutional_context: Head Start was launched in the spring of 1965 by the federal Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) as part of the War on Poverty, providing preschool education, meals, parenting services, and an unusually comprehensive set of health screenings and immunizations to poor 3- and 4-year-olds. Because Head Start funded local service providers directly rather than flowing through states, OEO worried that the most disadvantaged communities would lack capacity to write competitive grant proposals. In response, OEO sent Presidential Management Intern volunteers to the 300 poorest U.S. counties (defined by 1960 poverty rates) for several weeks to identify local sponsors, help draft applications, and shepherd them through OEO review. This grant-writing assistance was not extended to counties just below this poverty-rank threshold, and no other major federal social program used the same 300-county cutoff. The resulting gap in program funding and participation between counties just above and just below the cutoff persisted into the late 1970s before equalization rules eroded it.
